title: Cholesterol (atheroembolism) after angiography: highest risk is acute kidney injury
vignette: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to sudden-onset, severe abdominal pain accompanied by nausea. He has a history of coronary artery disease and recently underwent cardiac angiography. The patient is a current smoker with a 30-pack-year history. After initial evaluation, he undergoes emergency laparotomy. A segment of small intestine is resected. On microscopic examination, there are several large-caliber vessels with needle-shaped cholesterol clefts in their lumens, as shown in the image. Given these findings, the patient is at highest risk for which of the following complications?

clues.note: An invasive intra-arterial procedure (angiography) can mechanically dislodge aortic atherosclerotic plaque, showering cholesterol microemboli - atheroembolic disease.

clues.text: needle-shaped cholesterol clefts in their lumens
clues.note: Needle-shaped intravascular CHOLESTEROL CLEFTS (empty spaces where cholesterol dissolved during processing) are the diagnostic finding of atheroembolic (cholesterol crystal) embolism.

whatMatters: Sudden ischemia after an invasive vascular procedure with needle-shaped intravascular CHOLESTEROL CLEFTS = ATHEROEMBOLIC (cholesterol crystal) disease. Showered cholesterol microemboli lodge in small arteries; the KIDNEYS are the most commonly and severely affected organ -> ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY. Answer A.
strategy: Identify atheroembolism (cholesterol clefts after angiography) and recall the most common serious complication: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (emboli to arcuate/interlobular arteries). Other clues include blue-toe syndrome/livedo reticularis, GI ischemia (as here), and CNS events (amaurosis fugax). Reject myelosuppression (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is immune, not marrow), pulmonary infarction (extremely rare in atheroembolism), nephrolithiasis (unrelated), and septic arthritis (endocarditis - fever/bacteria, not cholesterol clefts).

eliminations.label: Myelosuppression - not the atheroembolism mechanism
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: bone marrow suppression causing cytopenias. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: heparin given during angiography can cause thrombocytopenia (HIT), but that is IMMUNE-mediated platelet destruction, not marrow suppression - and it isn't the atheroembolism risk. ✅ Correct if: a drug/marrow toxicity question.

eliminations.label: Nephrolithiasis - unrelated to cholesterol emboli
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: kidney stones. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: atheroembolism causes ischemic kidney INJURY, not stone formation. ✅ Correct if: a metabolic stone question.

eliminations.label: Pulmonary infarction - extremely rare here (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: infarction of lung tissue. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: pulmonary involvement in atheroembolic disease is EXTREMELY rare and far less common than acute kidney injury; cholesterol emboli from the aorta lodge in systemic (not pulmonary) arteries. ✅ Correct if: a venous thromboembolism/PE scenario.

eliminations.label: Septic arthritis - infective endocarditis, not cholesterol emboli
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a joint infection from embolic bacteria (infective endocarditis). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: endocarditis emboli contain bacteria (with fever/arthralgias/night sweats), not the sterile needle-shaped cholesterol clefts seen here. ✅ Correct if: infective endocarditis with septic emboli.

reasoning: Acute ischemia after an invasive vascular procedure (angiography) with intravascular cholesterol clefts = atheroembolic disease
Dislodged aortic plaque showers cholesterol-rich microemboli into small arteries
The kidneys (arcuate/interlobular arteries) are the most commonly and severely affected organ
-> highest risk for acute kidney injury; answer A
mechanism: Atheroembolic (cholesterol crystal embolization) disease occurs when an INVASIVE VASCULAR PROCEDURE (cardiac catheterization/angiography, aortic surgery) - or, less often, anticoagulation/thrombolysis - mechanically DISLODGES atherosclerotic plaque from large vessels such as the aorta, SHOWERING cholesterol-rich microemboli into the distal circulation. These emboli obstruct small arteries/arterioles, and cholesterol dissolves during tissue processing, leaving the characteristic NEEDLE-SHAPED CHOLESTEROL CLEFTS in vessel lumina (often with surrounding inflammation/giant cells). Clinical manifestations depend on where the emboli land; the KIDNEYS are most commonly and severely involved (partial/complete occlusion of arcuate and interlobular arteries -> ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY, often with eosinophilia/eosinophiluria and hypocomplementemia). Other affected sites include the SKIN (blue-toe syndrome, livedo reticularis), the GI tract (bleeding, intestinal infarction - as in this patient), and the CNS (stroke, amaurosis fugax). Therefore this patient is at highest risk for acute kidney injury. The distractors are complications of other processes (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, endocarditis emboli, venous thromboembolism, stones).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Path/CV > cholesterol (athero)embolism: after invasive vascular procedure; needle-shaped cholesterol clefts; most common serious complication = acute kidney injury; also blue-toe syndrome, livedo reticularis, GI ischemia, CNS events.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Cholesterol clefts after angiography = atheroembolism -> acute kidney injury (most affected organ).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on atheroembolism, cholesterol clefts, blue-toe syndrome, livedo reticularis, or eosinophiluria? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Myelosuppression (HIT is immune, not marrow), pulmonary infarction (rare), nephrolithiasis, septic arthritis (endocarditis) don't fit.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the histology: needle-shaped, empty (dissolved-cholesterol) clefts occluding small vessel lumina, sometimes with multinucleated giant cells. Anchor: 'needle-shaped cholesterol clefts = atheroembolism -> kidney injury.'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: atheroembolic disease = cholesterol clefts after vascular procedure; #1 complication acute kidney injury; blue-toe/livedo/GI/CNS.

keywords.front: Most common serious complication of atheroembolism

firstAid.detail: Path: cholesterol clefts after vascular procedure; acute kidney injury most common.
Path > HIT (immune), PE, endocarditis (septic emboli), stones.
CV > blue-toe syndrome, livedo reticularis, GI/CNS ischemia.

memoryHook: Catheter scrapes the aorta, showering cholesterol needles downstream - they clog the kidney's small arteries first, so acute kidney injury is the top risk (blue toes and gut ischemia tag along).
